analysis.body:
# Grid Queues and Data Center Power

The US interconnection queues contain 1.33 trillion watts of planned generation and storage across five major grid operators, with 8,377 total projects awaiting connection as of mid-September 2026. ERCOT dominates by capacity with 438 gigawatts in Texas alone, followed by NYISO at 319 gigawatts. Gas-fired capacity across all queues totals roughly 184 gigawatts, while battery storage represents 327 gigawatts—together these flexible resources signal grid operators' preparation for variable load. These queue totals measure power generation and storage in development, not data center demand itself, but the rapid growth in battery and gas capacity historically tracks demand from large industrial loads like AI facilities.

Commercial-sector electricity sales in eight key states reached 54.8 terawatt-hours in the second quarter of 2026, with Texas consuming 15.8 terawatt-hours at the lowest average price of $8.66 per megawatt-hour, while California consumed 10 terawatt-hours at $27.33 per megawatt-hour. Data centers are billed within the commercial class but are not separately metered in these figures, making this a proxy indicator rather than a direct measure of facility load. Texas and California together account for roughly half of the eight-state total, reflecting their established roles as grid-scale computing hubs.

Solar comprises the largest single fuel type in the queues at 329 gigawatts, yet storage and gas together now nearly equal solar capacity—a shift that reflects grid operators' focus on reliability during peak AI training workloads rather than pure renewable volume. Watch the ratio of storage-to-solar additions in ERCOT and CAISO queues over the next reporting cycle, as this ratio will indicate whether grid operators expect data center load growth to accelerate beyond current interconnection forecasts.
